source_text: Sed currant ad eum qui clamat: Iugum meum suave est, et onus meum leve est [n299] ; qui et malae voluntati veniam pro inaestimabili liberalitate largitur, et innocentiam, quam creat bonam, facit innovando adoptandoque meliorem.
pass_a_gloss: But let them run to him who cries: My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light; who both by inestimable liberality lavishes pardon on an evil will, and the innocence, which he creates good, he makes better by renewing and adopting.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Rather, let them run to the one who cries: “My yoke is gentle and my burden light” (Matthew 11:30). With immeasurable generosity he both grants pardon to an evil will and, through renewal and adoption, makes better the innocence that he creates good.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
